title: Psalm 113: The High God Who Stoops Low
summary: The servants of the LORD are called to praise his name at all times and in every place. He is exalted above the nations and the heavens, yet he stoops to look on the earth, lifts the poor from the dust to sit with princes, and gives the childless woman a home full of children.
story: Psalm 113 opens the Egyptian Hallel, the group of Psalms 113 to 118 that Jewish tradition sang at the great festivals and especially at Passover, the feast remembering the exodus from Egypt. Hallel means praise, and these six psalms praise the God who rescued his people. Coming after the twin wisdom psalms 111 and 112, Psalm 113 broadens the view: the God who acted for Israel is the same God enthroned above all nations, and his greatness shows itself in how far down he reaches. It prepares for Psalm 114, which tells the exodus itself.
historical:
The psalm has no author in its heading and begins and ends with “Hallelujah!” Its date is uncertain. Some scholars see it as old temple hymnody, others as part of the post-exilic shaping of Book V; the psalm's content fits any period of Israel's worship. Its closest relative is the song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2:1-10, which also speaks of God raising the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to seat them with princes, and of the barren woman bearing children. Whether the psalm drew on Hannah's song, or both drew on a common stock of praise, cannot be known.

The association with Passover is well attested. The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish legal tradition compiled around AD 200, describes the Hallel being sung at the Passover meal, with part sung before the meal and the rest after it. The practice was probably older than its written record, and many interpreters think Jesus and his disciples sang these psalms at the Last Supper.
cultural:
The ash heap or refuse dump (the BSB's “dump” in verse 7) lay outside a town, where rubbish and dung were burned. It was where outcasts, beggars, and the diseased might sit, the lowest place in the community. To be lifted from there to sit with nobles was the most dramatic social reversal an ancient reader could imagine.

The barren woman of verse 9 would have been felt with equal force. In Israel, as across the ancient world, childlessness brought grief, social shame, and economic insecurity, since children cared for parents in old age and carried on the family name. Israel's story is full of such women whom God gave children: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and later Elizabeth. The phrase from where the sun rises to where it sets, in verse 3, is a way of saying everywhere, east to west, and possibly always, from morning to evening.
literary: The psalm is a hymn of praise in three parts. Verses 1 to 3 call the servants of the LORD to praise his name, with the word praise repeated and the name of the LORD named three times. Verses 4 to 6 lift the eye upward to God enthroned above the nations and the heavens, and then turn on the question “Who is like the LORD our God?” with the surprising answer that the one enthroned on high stoops to look far below. Verses 7 to 9 follow him down to the poor, the needy, and the barren. The movement of the poem mirrors its theme: it rises to the highest point and then descends to the lowest, and the praise is found in the descent. The psalm is framed by Hallelujah at beginning and end.

outline.t: Praise the name of the LORD at all times and everywhere
Who is like the LORD, enthroned on high yet stooping low?
He lifts the poor and gives the barren a home

doctrines.note: God is both transcendent, far above all creation, and near, stooping to see and help. The psalm refuses to separate his greatness from his kindness; his exalted position is exactly what makes his care for the lowly remarkable.
Salvation here looks like reversal: the poor seated with princes, the barren made a joyful mother. God's rescue lifts people from shame into honor and belonging.
The call to praise stretches from east to west, and God is exalted over all the nations. The worship of Israel has the whole world in view.

words.note: Shafel, to be low or to bring low. In verse 6 the form describes God making himself low in order to see, rendered “He humbles Himself to behold.” The word is used elsewhere for humbling the proud; here the high God chooses lowness in order to look after his creatures.

Afar, dust. It is the stuff from which Adam was formed (Genesis 2:7) and to which people return in death. Being raised from the dust means rescue from the lowest human condition, and it can carry overtones of new life.

Aqar, barren. The word describes the childless woman whose grief runs through Israel's story, from Sarah (Genesis 11:30) to Hannah. God's gift of children to such women repeatedly marks a new turn in his purposes.

Shem, name. The name of the LORD is praised three times in verses 1 to 3. In the Old Testament a name expresses a person's character and presence, so praising God's name means honoring who he has shown himself to be.

christ: Many interpreters believe that Jesus and his disciples sang this psalm and the rest of the Hallel at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30 says they sang a hymn before going out to the Mount of Olives). The psalm's pattern of the high God stooping low is fulfilled in the incarnation: Paul describes Christ, who was in the form of God, humbling himself to become a servant and to die (Philippians 2:5-8). Mary's song in Luke 1:46-55 echoes the same reversal as Psalm 113 and Hannah's song, praising God who has brought down rulers and lifted up the humble, and her own child and her relative Elizabeth's son, born to a woman long barren, are signs that God was stooping once more.
questions: The psalm finds God's greatness in how far down he reaches. How does this change the way you think about God's power?
Who in your community sits on the ash heap, and what would it look like to share God's concern to seat them with princes?
The psalm calls for praise from sunrise to sunset. What would it mean to let praise fill the ordinary hours of your day?
